summary: At fifty square miles, Ontario is one of the Inland Empire's genuine job centers rather than a pure bedroom community — Ontario International Airport, a massive logistics corridor along the I-10 and I-15 interchange, and the Ontario Mills shopping complex together anchor an employment base heavy on warehousing, distribution, and transportation, meaning a significant share of workers can commute locally rather than grinding west toward Los Angeles. That infrastructure backbone cuts both ways: the freeway interchange and rail lines carve the city into distinct zones, so moving between a quiet residential stretch near the foothills and a commercial area south of the 10 can feel like crossing into a different town entirely. The San Gabriel Mountains rise sharply to the north, giving clear-day views of snow-capped peaks and putting trailheads within a short drive, while the city itself sits on a broad, flat alluvial plain — expect wide streets, open sky, and relentless sunshine averaging 9.6 hours a day with summer highs routinely in the mid-90s. At a median income of roughly $83,000 against a median home price of $568,000, the price-to-income ratio hovers near 6.9 — tight but notably more accessible than coastal Southern California. Ontario is essentially a logistics economy wrapped in a sunbaked grid, where proximity to two major freeways is both the greatest convenience and the defining tradeoff.
